units.spoken: Q-Learning
Learn how good each choice is, one try at a time.
A robot that only knows how good each spot is still cannot pick a step unless it knows where every step leads. How can it choose well without that?

The agent is the learner that picks the moves, as taught in RL Basics. A state is the agent's situation right now; a move, or action, is one choice the agent can make in a state; a reward is the number the world hands back after each move, good or bad, as taught in RL Basics. Here the agent is a warehouse robot that must reach its charging dock. It starts in one bottom corner and the dock sits in the other. The floor is a grid of cells, one per place the robot can stand. It knows only which cell it stands in, not where each move leads or what it costs.

Take a look at this figure. The robot begins knowing nothing at all, and that is the point. Every move wears a question mark because no score exists yet for any of them, so the robot has no reason to prefer one move over another. The ledge sits between the start and the dock, so the shortest way is also the most expensive one, and the robot cannot know that until it tries. Learning here means turning those question marks into scores, one tried move at a time.

Figure 1 shows the floor the robot learns on: four rows by twelve columns, the robot at bottom left and the dock at bottom right. The red squares are the ledge, the green square is the dock, and the question marks stand on moves the robot has not tried yet. Take the robot at the start: every move wears a question mark, since no score exists yet for any of them.
An episode is one run from the start until it ends, as taught in RL Basics. The ledge is the strip of floor between the start and the dock. Reaching the dock can take many moves.

Each move's reward is minus the battery it uses, so the best total is the one closest to zero. Every move costs a little battery; stepping onto the ledge costs a lot and puts the robot back at the start; only reaching the dock ends the episode. The cheapest way to the dock is the shortest path that never steps onto the ledge.
Section one, Scores for moves, not just for places

A move is only worth making if what follows it is worth having. The return is all the reward still to come, with later rewards counted a little less, as taught in RL Basics. A state's value is the return the agent expects from state, as taught in RL Basics. A policy is the agent's rule for choosing a move in each state; it may always pick the same move or pick by chance, as taught in RL Basics. On this floor every value is below zero, because every step costs battery.

Knowing how good a spot is does not yet say which step to take. A model is the agent's learned guess of where a move leads and what it pays, as taught in RL Method Families. A move's value, also called its score, is the return the agent expects if it makes move in state and plays on from there, as taught in RL Basics. Epsilon-greedy usually plays the top-scored move and, with chance epsilon, a random one instead, as taught in RL Basics. From a cell away from the walls, each of the four moves leads to a different neighbouring cell.

What this loop is teaching is that learning here is one small change at a time, repeated. Each trip around the loop changes exactly one score, the score of the move just played, and nothing else moves. The robot does not plan the whole route at once and it does not wait until the episode ends; it learns from the step it just took, right away. Run that loop enough times and the scores settle into the cheap route, because every step that paid off nudges its score up and every step that cost too much nudges its score down.

Figure 2 shows the loop the robot runs on every step, from standing in a cell to changing one score. Each box is one stage: pick a move, take it and pay its cost, judge it by its reward plus how good the next cell looks, then change that score. The repeat arrow sends the loop back to the start. Take a step toward the dock: the loop picks the move, pays its cost, judges it against the next cell, and nudges that move's score.

Best play is the policy that earns the most return; the best-play score is each move's value under it, as taught in RL Basics. The robot learns these scores only from its own steps, one cell at a time.

RL Basics taught how to improve a cell's value. To choose a move from the value alone, the robot would need to know where each move leads, which is a model it does not have. A score for each move, lets it choose by comparing scores, with no model at all. And it wants the scores of best play, not of whatever it happens to do now.
Section two, A table of move scores
One score per cell and move
Picture the floor as a table: one row per cell, one column per move, every entry a guess of its score.
Compare the four scores in the robot's row; the top one is the move to play.
When it works, the robot picks its best move by reading the table.
A score to aim at
Picture the robot after one step: the target is the number its score is pulled toward.
Build the target from the step just taken, not from the whole episode.
When it works, each score is pulled toward what best play would earn there, so the table climbs toward the best route.
Take the best of what follows
Picture the landing cell: its four moves carry four scores, and the target takes only the best.
Look at the landing cell, not the cell the robot just left.
When it works, the target aims at best play while the robot wanders, so the scores end at best play.
A tabular method stores one entry per state, or per state and move. So a step only ever changes the one entry it played.

Take a look at this figure. The table and the floor are the same knowledge in two forms, and that is the point. Each cell holds a score for each of its four moves, and the shading is the score, so the whole floor becomes a picture of what the robot has learned. The brightness climbs toward the dock because the moves that end the episode cheapest carry the best scores, and the ledge stays dark because stepping there costs the most. The robot's knowledge is a landscape that slopes toward the dock.

Figure 3 shows the table itself: every cell split into a triangle per move, shaded by that move's score. Brighter triangles mean less battery still to spend, so the bright cells sit near the dock and the ledge stays red. Take the cell just above the dock: its downward triangle shines brightest, since that move ends the episode cheapest.
The discount sets how much a reward one step later still counts.

An expected value is the average over everything that can happen by chance, weighted by how likely each outcome is, as taught in Expected value and RL Basics. The sign marks an expected value, as taught in Probability. On this floor the average hardly matters, because the same move from the same cell always has the same result.
Take the robot in the cell just above the dock. Best play is to step down onto the dock, and that move's score is minus the cost of that last step.
Equation 1. The robot has no model of the floor, so it cannot score a move by looking ahead to where it leads.
Take a look at this equation. It says what a move is worth under best play.

The target line. Y star sub t is the best-play target at step t. R sub t plus one is the reward the move just paid. Gamma is the discount, how much a later reward still counts. Q star scores move a in the next cell. The max picks the next cell's best move. The target is the reward plus the discounted best score from there, and the guess is pulled toward it. Intuitively, the best target is the pay now plus the best pay from the landing.
Intuition. The move value scores one move played first, while the spot value averages over the moves best play picks.
Example. Take the move down onto the dock: it ends the episode, so its target is the step's reward alone.

The score line. Q star scores the cell and move just played. E, the expectation, averages what the floor might return. The bar means given this cell and this move. The score equals the expected value of y star sub t, the target, given this cell and this move. The average is a sum: each outcome times its chance, added up. Intuitively, a move's score is its target's average.
Intuition. The spot value averages over the moves best play picks first, while the move value pins one move first.
Example. Take a move that stays on the floor: its score averages the target over the one landing the floor returns, the step's reward plus the best score from there.

A move that stays on the floor lands on a cell whose best next score still counts, so its target adds the discounted best score from there. The two moves from that cell carry different targets because they land in different cells.
On this floor that makes the best scores climb toward zero as the cells get closer to the dock.
Section three, Aiming every score at best play
Move a little, not all the way
Picture the played entry: it moves a little toward its target, never all at once.
How. Each step moves one entry a little, and the next step moves the next one.
When it works, the scores creep toward best play step by step.

Bootstrapping means putting the robot's own current guess for the next state inside the target, as taught in RL Basics. The TD (temporal difference) error is how much one step surprised the agent, the target minus the current guess, as taught in RL Basics. A fall is a step onto the ledge: the robot pays the big cost and goes back to the start, so it must walk the whole floor again.

The learning rate sets how big a step each update takes, as taught in RL Basics. The robot steps along an aisle toward the dock and pays a little battery; it judges that move by its reward plus the best it believes it can do from the new cell.

Argmax picks the move whose score is largest, as taught in RL Basics. The greedy policy plays the top-scored move in each state. While the scores are still guesses, the top entry can point the wrong way, and the next steps correct it.
Equation 2. The table holds guesses, not best-play scores, so the target must be built from what the table holds now.
Take a look at this equation. It nudges each score toward its target, one small step at a time.

The reward line. Y sub t is the target at step t. R sub t plus one is the reward the move just paid. The reward arrives with the next cell. The guess is pulled toward the target. The target is the reward alone when the move ends the episode. Without the star, the target is built from the table's guesses. Intuitively, the target starts with the pay the move just earned.
Example. Take the move down onto the dock: the target is just the step's reward, since the episode ends there.

The landing line. Gamma is the discount, how much a later reward still counts. Q, the table's score, rates move a in the next cell. The plus adds the landing's worth to the reward. The max picks the next cell's best move. One step gives one landing and one target, so nothing is averaged. A fall still builds its target: the robot pays, goes back, and the episode goes on. Intuitively, the target adds what the landing is worth.
Intuition. The second half of the target is that landing's best score.
Example. Take a step that stays on the floor: the target adds the discounted best score of the cell it lands on to the step's reward.

The surprise line. Delta sub t is the surprise at step t. Q, the table's score, is the guess for the move just played. The minus is the gap between the target and the guess. A positive surprise means the guess must rise, a negative one means it must fall. The surprise is one step's, not the whole episode's. Intuitively, the surprise says how far the guess missed, and in which direction.
Example. Take a step whose target sits above the score the table holds: the surprise is positive, so the guess must rise.

The update line. Q, the table's score, is the played entry. Eta is the learning rate, how big each step is. Delta sub t is the surprise, the gap the step just found. The arrow says replace: the old entry goes away. The plus adds a share of the surprise, never the whole surprise. Intuitively, one step moves the played entry a little, never all the way.
Example. Take the step toward the dock whose target sits above its score: the entry moves up by a share of the surprise, and the rest of the table stays put.

The greedy line. Pi greedy takes a cell and returns its top-scored move. Q, the table's score, rates each move in the cell. Argmax scans the four moves and returns the one whose score is largest. The greedy policy equals the argmax of the table's scores. While learning, the robot follows epsilon-greedy, so a random move sometimes replaces the top-scored one. Intuitively, the greedy policy turns scores into a choice.
Intuition. Once the scores are nudged, the robot plays the best one.
Example. Take the robot in a cell where one move's score stands above the rest: the greedy policy plays that move, unless a random move is drawn instead.

Take a step toward the dock from the cell above it, where the target comes out above the score the table holds. The surprise is positive, so the entry for that cell and move is nudged upward by a share of the surprise, while every other entry stays as it was. The next time the robot stands in that cell, the top-scored move is read off the nudged table, and the same five lines run again.

The target never uses the move epsilon-greedy will pick next, only the best one, so random exploring moves change which steps the robot takes but not what the target aims at; that is why the table ends at best-play scores. Off-policy means learning the values of one policy while playing another. Q-learning is off-policy, since it learns best play while it plays epsilon-greedy. One step costs little: a max over the four moves in the next cell, then one write to the table.
Section four, A step on the floor and the score it nudges

What this figure is teaching is that one update touches exactly one thing. The bars are the scores where the robot stands, and when the walk reaches stage 7 only the played move's bar moves, part of the way toward its target, while every other bar stays exactly where it was. That is the whole update: one step, one bar, one small move. The stages walk the equation in order, so each line of the equation has a moment in the walk, and the bar you watch is the entry the line changes.

Step through the walk with Next and watch the bars. Each stage uses one line, and at stage 7 only the played move's bar moves, part of the way toward its target. Try the exploring step and watch the fall cost far more than the table thought, then the last step, where the reward alone is the target.

Figure 4 shows one update: battery bars hanging down, with the walkthrough card below it. Each bar is one move's score where the robot stands. Stage 1 is the robot standing in its cell, stage 2 the move it picks, stage 3 the floor answering with a reward and a landing cell, stage 4 the landing cell's best score marked, stage 5 the target built from that reward and best score, stage 6 the gap between target and guess, and stage 7 the played entry moving part of the way toward its target.
Equation 2 again, walked one stage at a time. One real step on the floor becomes one small change in what the robot believes, so a tried move looks better or worse next time.
Take a look at this equation. It is the same update, walked one stage at a time.

Stage 4, the reward line. Y sub t is the target at step t. R sub t plus one is the pay this step earned. On the last step the walk ends here, and the target is the reward alone. Intuitively, this line is the pay the step earned.
Example. Take the walk's last step, the move down onto the dock: the episode ends, so no landing score joins the reward.

Stage 5, the landing line. Gamma is the discount, and here it is one. Q, the table's score, rates move a in the landing cell. The best score is not discounted. The plus completes the target across stages 4 and 5. The max picks the landing cell's best move. One step gives one landing and one target, so nothing is averaged. A fall still builds a target, and the walk goes on. Intuitively, the target is finished with the landing's best score.
Intuition. At stages 4 and 5 the walk looks at the square the robot landed on and takes the best score there, which becomes the target's second half.
Example. Take the ordinary step at stage 5: it lands one square right, so the target adds the best score of that square.

Stage 6, the surprise line. Delta sub t is the surprise at step t. Q, the table's score, is the guess for the move just played. The minus is the gap between the target and the guess. A positive surprise means the guess must rise, a negative one means it must fall. Intuitively, the surprise says how far the guess missed, and in which direction.
Intuition. Stage 6 of the walk is the reckoning: the target and the guess are set side by side, and the gap between them is this step's surprise.
Example. Take the exploring step at stage 6: the fall cost far more than the table thought, so the gap is large and negative.

Stage 7, the update line. Q, the table's score, is the played entry. Eta is the learning rate, how big each step is. Delta sub t is the surprise, the gap the step just found. The arrow says replace: the old entry goes away. The plus moves the bar a share of the gap, never all the way. Intuitively, one step moves the played bar a little, never all the way.
Intuition. Stage 7 is where the walk changes the table: the played bar moves part of the way toward its target, and every other bar stays where it was.
Example. Take the exploring step at stage 7: its bar grows a long way toward the target, and the other bars stay put.

The greedy line. Pi greedy takes a cell and returns its top-scored move. Q, the table's score, rates each move in the cell. Argmax scans the four moves and returns the one whose score is largest. The greedy policy equals the argmax of the table's scores. While learning, the robot follows epsilon-greedy around this policy. Intuitively, the greedy policy turns scores into a choice. So the walk is one idea: aim, nudge, and play the top-scored move.
Intuition. The walk ends with the choice the nudged table makes.
Example. Take the next step the walkthrough shows: the robot reads the top-scored move off the nudged table and plays it, unless a random move is drawn.

Section six, How the starting scores steer the robot

That hopeful start sends the robot to untried moves first. The robot's route is the path its best moves trace from the start, drawn as arrows in Figure 5; it counts only if it reaches the dock without a loop. A gloomy start puts every score far below any real score; once one route reaches the dock its scores rise above all the others, so the robot can keep that first route even when a shorter one exists.

The starting scores decide the route before the robot has learned anything, and that is the point. A gloomy start sets every score to a number far smaller than any real score, so the first route that reaches the dock beats all the others and the robot keeps it, even when a shorter route exists, because it never tries the moves that would find it. A hopeful start does the opposite: untried moves look best, so the robot tries them first. The lesson is that learning is path-dependent: what the robot finds first shapes what it keeps.

Set the start to Gloomy and the exploring to some, then press Play and watch the route. The robot locks in the first route it finds, a longer one, because its scores rise above the rest before it tries anything shorter. Switch the start to Zero and watch it try untried moves first.

Figure 5 shows how the starting scores steer the robot: the floor shaded by the best score in each cell, with arrows for the best move. The dashed line traces the route the arrows draw from the start. Take the Gloomy start with some exploring: the dashed line shows the longer way around. The exploring buttons set how often the robot tries a random move while it learns.
Section seven, Updating after every step, and exploring less over time
Wander early, trust the table late
Picture the robot early on: every score is a guess, so it tries untested moves; late on, it mostly plays its top-scored move.
How. The shrink happens once per episode, at its end, not after every step.
When it works, early wandering finds the dock and late play follows the best route.

Q-learning updates after every step, while the episode is still going. It learns online, from a stream of moves, and never has to store whole episodes or wait for them to end. There is no batch of steps to gather and no network to train. A network is a fitted set of numbers that guesses a score for any cell and move, instead of storing one entry for each.

The table is a NumPy array, indexed by cell and move. Every score starts at zero, as How the starting scores steer the robot explains. Only reaching the dock ends the episode, so only that step uses the step's reward alone.
Equation 3. The robot explores a lot early, when every score is a guess, and mostly plays its top-scored move only once the chance has shrunk to its floor, when the scores have settled.
Take a look at this equation. It shrinks the exploring chance a little after every episode, but never below its floor.

The shrink line. Epsilon is the exploring chance, the share of random moves. Kappa is the decay factor, just under one. Epsilon min is the floor, the smallest the chance ever gets. The arrow says replace: the old chance goes away. Max picks the larger, so the shrink ends at the floor. Each episode multiplies the chance by kappa, so it shrinks a little. Intuitively, exploring shrinks a little after every episode, but never below a floor.
Example. Take the robot early in training, when its exploring chance is still high: it tries untested moves often, and the chance shrinks a little after each episode.

Take the robot early in training, when its exploring chance is still high and it tries untested moves often, and late in training, when the chance has shrunk but is still well above its floor, so it wanders often and plays its top-scored move more than at the start. The shrink never reaches zero, so even late in training the robot tries a random move now and then, and a move it has never tried can still be found.

What this curve is teaching is that the exploring chance falls slowly, much more slowly than the learning. After 200 episodes it is still about two-thirds, so the robot still tries a random move on most steps even though it has already found a good route. The shrink multiplies by a number just under one each episode, so the fall flattens, and the floor of 0.01 would take about 2,300 episodes to reach. Wandering does not stop when learning settles, and that is why it still steps off the ledge.

Figure 6 shows the exploring chance falling as episodes go on, from mostly random moves toward mostly top-scored moves. The curve falls from 1.0 to about 0.67 over 200 episodes, staying well above the dashed line, the minimum, which the chance never drops below. Episodes run along the bottom, and the height is the chance of a random move. Take the robot after 200 episodes: the chance is still about two-thirds, so it still wanders often; the floor of 0.01 would take about 2,300 episodes to reach.

Section eight, When a table is enough

A table is enough when the cells are few and the moves are few enough to list, so every entry is tried often. This floor has 48 cells and 4 moves, 192 entries in all, and 200 episodes of steps cover them again and again. When the floor grows, most entries are never tried, and the table stays a guess.

A theorem says the scores settle on the best-play scores if every move is tried often enough in every cell, with one entry per cell and move, and if the learning rate shrinks so the sum of its steps grows without bound while the sum of their squares stays finite. The proof comes from Watkins and Dayan, named in the references. This page keeps the learning rate fixed at 0.5, a practical choice that does not meet the theorem's shrinking condition.
